title: The Protocol Your Team Is Missing
author: Honest Office
summary: In this piece the writer, an L&D practitioner at Honest Office, borrows a structured group problem-solving format from K-12 school reform -- the Problem of Practice (or Consultancy) protocol -- and argues it belongs in every workplace, not just schools. Developed decades ago at the Coalition of Essential Schools for teachers facing messy, under-resourced dilemmas, the protocol assigns roles (Presenter, Facilitator, Consultants) and moves through clarifying questions, probing questions, and a listen-only reflection period. The author's central claim is that organizational learning cultures are biased toward content delivery -- courses, workshops, LMS modules -- when what teams actually need is a disciplined space to think through real problems together. Having used the protocol on their own team, the author found it surfaced pain points a normal check-in never would have, and left the Presenter with a reframed understanding of their own problem rather than a canned answer. The piece closes by framing Problem of Practice as an easy, cost-free upgrade to any existing meeting.
points: The Problem of Practice (Consultancy) protocol, borrowed from K-12 school-reform circles, structures a 30-40 minute meeting around defined roles (Presenter, Facilitator, Consultants) so a stuck colleague gets probing questions rather than premature advice.
The protocol's core discipline is silence: the Presenter cannot respond while Consultants discuss the problem aloud, which forces listening for understanding rather than listening to rebut.
The author argues most workplace learning cultures over-invest in content delivery (courses, LMS) and under-invest in structured peer problem-solving, which this protocol corrects cheaply.
Running the protocol surfaces problems nobody had named yet, because the Presenter's own understanding of the issue often shifts by the end of the session.
quotes: The Problem of Practice protocol, originally developed by Gene Thompson-Grove, Paula Evans, and Faith Dunne at the Coalition of Essential Schools and the Annenberg Institute for School Reform, was designed for educators working in complex, under-resourced environments with myriad issues and unclear solutions.
Largely speaking, many organizations have learning cultures with deep, structural biases towards content delivery

This is the heart of the protocol, and probably the most difficult part for everyone. Consultants ask deeper, more probing questions, with the aim of helping the group understand the problem more fully.
Not only are we able to generate more free-flowing ideas this way, but we're listening for the sake of listening, rather than listening to respond and missing out on valuable information as a result.

When team meetings are 45 minutes of status updates led by one person and 15 minutes of talking in circles hurriedly, most people walk away feeling bored, confused, frustrated, or some combination of the three.
The Problem of Practice protocol has been utilized in schools for years, and I believe it's high time for us to bring it into learning and organizational development.
